messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 21
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Public Defender
- Trauma Type: Refugee
- Pcl5: 62

The sirens still pull him under. He is nineteen again when the borders close. His father tells him to pack only what fits in a backpack and to leave the photographs on the table. They walk through snow that melts into slush and then into mud, crossing checkpoints where men in fatigues ask for papers he does not have. He remembers the smell of diesel and wet wool, the way his younger sister’s fingers dig into his jacket, the constant scanning of the tree line. When they finally reach the camp, he stops believing that tomorrow will look like yesterday. At twenty-one, he sits across from me in a chair that angles slightly toward the door. He wears a dark suit to court each morning, tie knotted tight, as if armor requires structure. His office at the public defender’s office is on the third floor, past the holding cells, past the fluorescent hum that vibrates in his molars. He reads case files with precise, unhurried strokes, but when a witness describes a domestic assault, his jaw tightens. He exhales slowly, presses his thumb to his index finger, and continues reading. He has learned to keep his voice level, to meet the eyes of the judge without flinching when the gavel cracks. Still, he counts the exits in every room. At a recent hearing, a fire alarm tests the building’s wiring; he is at the stairwell before anyone else registers the sound. His partner wakes first sometimes, just to check if he is breathing steadily. They have been together for eleven months. She says he feels present during coffee, during walks along the river, but that the night pulls him under. He does not dream so much as rehearse. He lies awake tracing the seam of the ceiling, listening for the floorboards of the apartment above to settle. When a car backfires outside, his heart hammers against his ribs before his mind catches up. He has learned not to apologize for the jump. He simply turns toward her, matches his breathing to hers, and waits for the noise to dissolve into the street. He tells her he knows he should sleep through it. He tells her he will. Neither of them says it is the same lie he tells himself every morning. Defending indigent clients has not softened the edges of his memories; it has given them a new shape. He sits in rooms where young men explain why they broke into pharmacies, why they ran, why they stayed silent. He takes notes. He files motions. He argues bail. He does not flinch when the word border comes up in testimony. Instead, he listens for the fractures in the story, the gaps where fear lived. He tells me that sometimes, when he stacks the file folders, the paper cuts feel like proof he is still here. He does not know how to explain that safety feels like a language he has yet to learn, only memorize. He arrives on time. He answers the phone. He shows up.
